prompt: Should students be required to learn a second language? Write an essay taking a position.
text:
# Why Schools Should Require a Second Language

Most students in English-speaking countries can finish school without ever learning to speak another language. I think that is a mistake. Schools should require every student to study a second language for several years, because the benefits are real, they reach beyond the classroom, and no other subject offers quite the same combination.

The usual objection is practical. English is already the dominant language of science, business and the internet, so why spend hundreds of hours on Spanish or Mandarin? Translation software is also getting better every year. But this objection treats language class as job training for one skill, and it isn't that. Learning a language trains attention, memory and the ability to notice patterns. Studies of bilingual people often find that they switch between tasks more easily and ignore distractions better. Researchers still argue about how large these effects are, so I won't claim that a language class makes anyone smarter. The safer claim is that it is hard, structured mental work, and students gain from doing hard work.

The stronger argument is about understanding other people. When you learn a language, you find out that other people don't just use different words for the same ideas. Some languages have no word for a feeling you thought was universal. Others make you state things English lets you skip, such as whether you saw an event yourself or only heard about it. Seeing this firsthand is the best cure I know for the assumption that your own way of saying things is the natural one. Translation software can give you the meaning of a sentence, but it cannot give you that experience.

A language requirement also helps students understand English. Most students never think about grammar in their native language, because they never had to. Once they have to learn what a subject, a tense or a clause is in order to write French, they start to see how English works too. Many teachers report that this carries over into better writing.

Then there is fairness. If a language is optional, the students who take it tend to be those whose families already value it, or whose schools can afford the teachers. A requirement gives every student the same opportunity, including those who would never have chosen it and might discover a talent or an interest they didn't know they had.

The requirement has to be done well, though, and this is where the critics have a point. Many students sit through years of classes and still can't hold a basic conversation. That is a failure of teaching, not a reason to drop the subject. Schools should start early, since young children learn languages more easily. They should also let students choose among several languages, and they should measure success by what students can actually do: read a short article, order a meal, follow a conversation. Memorizing verb tables for a test does not count.

Some students will struggle, and a few have learning difficulties that make a language very hard. Schools should offer them adapted goals or alternatives, such as a focus on listening and speaking over written grammar. A rule with sensible exceptions is still a rule worth having.

In the end, the case is simple. A required language gives students a hard skill to practice, a clearer view of their own language and a way into other cultures. English speakers in particular can easily forget how much of the world lives in other languages. A school system that wants to prepare students for that world should make sure each of them learns at least one.
